text:
What does it take to engineer an AI
customer support platform that can serve

multiple businesses while keeping their
knowledge, conversations,
and customer data isolated?

This case study shows the working product,
the architecture behind it,

what broke along the way, and what is
still unproven.

Customers ask the same questions again and
again.

The answers usually exist, spread across
policy documents and web pages,
but someone has to find them each time.

A support assistant grounded in a
business's own material can help.

And if one shared platform serves many
separate businesses,

every answer has to come from the right
one, and only that one.

Here is the real application, running
locally with fictional data.

An owner signs in and lands on the
organization dashboard.
A short wizard creates a chatbot.

Documents are uploaded, and a background
worker takes each one from queued,
to processing, to ready.

You can inspect the passages it produced
and test which ones a question retrieves.

Websites can be added too; here the
crawler refuses a private network address.

In the playground, a question streams back
with a numbered source.
One important note:
this is a deterministic demonstration.

The reply is a fixed sentence, not an AI
answer.

What is real is the retrieval, the
streaming and the citation.

An unrelated question gets a fallback
instead.

Once the bot is active and the website's
origin is verified,

a visitor asks through the embedded
widget.

The team sees that conversation in the
inbox, marks it resolved,
and analytics update from stored events.
The system is a modular monolith:

one Python codebase and one database, run
as several processes.

That is not microservices, even though
there are several containers.

The Next.js and React dashboard talks to a
FastAPI backend over ordinary requests.

Dashboard requests are authenticated and
checked against the member's role.

Chat answers come back from the same API
as a stream of server-sent events.

The widget on a customer's site is a small
loader that opens an isolated frame.

PostgreSQL holds relational data and
vectors, using the pgvector extension.

Private object storage keeps the original
files.

Language and embedding models sit behind
provider adapters.
Slow work leaves the request path.

Redis carries the queue to Celery workers,
which parse, chunk and embed documents.

A scheduler triggers a recovery sweep on
its own maintenance worker,
so busy ingestion cannot delay it.
Everything runs in Docker containers.

Retrieval augmented generation means
finding evidence first,
then writing from it.

A file or web page is extracted into text,
cleaned,

and split into overlapping chunks that
never cross a heading.

Each chunk gets an embedding, a list of
numbers, stored beside the text.
A question is searched two ways:

vector search compares embeddings, keyword
search matches words,
and the two rankings are merged.

Retrieval is always scoped to one
organization and one chatbot.

The prompt is assembled, the model
streams,

and citations are validated on the way
out.

Citation provenance proves a source was
shown to the model,
not that it supports the sentence.

Offline, with a word-matching stand-in for
embeddings,

the answer appeared in the top five for
eighty-five percent of cases,
below the ninety percent target.
Real model accuracy is untested.
Take two fictional businesses.

Each has its own chatbot, documents and
conversations.

Here the second owner opens the first
one's address,
and gets organization not found.
Several layers enforce this.

Sessions live on the server, in a cookie
scripts cannot read.
Roles decide what each member may do.
Queries are scoped to the organization,

and PostgreSQL enforces forced row-level
security underneath,

so a missed filter is not enough to leak a
row.

Public widgets receive short-lived tokens
limited to one conversation,

and visitors get only the fields they
need.

Forwarding headers are trusted only from
listed proxies,
and AI providers must use HTTPS.

This is tested design, not a security
certification.

An audit then found problems that the
existing, passing tests had missed.

First, ten simultaneous chats exhausted
the database connection pool.

Each request held one connection while
asking for another.

The fix releases it early, keeps
transactions short,
and queues or refuses extra work.

At one hundred concurrent requests, sixty-
seven were served,

thirty-three were politely refused, and
none failed.

Second, a source cut from the prompt could
still be cited.

Now only sources actually rendered can be
cited, even midway through a stream.

Third, a hostile document could tie up a
worker.

Each parse now runs in a fresh process
with time and memory limits,

and a failed attempt leaves the previous
version in place.

That is containment, not yet a security
sandbox.
Fourth, found while fixing that one,

a stale crawl could overwrite newer stored
pages.
Every write now gets a new object key,

published only by the attempt that still
owns the job.

The widget has to behave on websites it
does not control.

Adding the same script twice keeps one
instance.
A second instance must be asked for.

Destroying it removes the frame and its
listener,

so single-page applications can remount
safely.

An anonymous visitor's conversation
resumes after a reload,

and an interrupted answer is recorded as
interrupted.
It adapts to a phone screen.

The loader is five thousand two hundred
and forty-eight bytes compressed,

against a budget of ten thousand two
hundred and forty.
These journeys were tested in Chrome only.
The method was audit driven.

Build the initial system, measure a
baseline, record findings,

fix one at a time with a failing test
first where possible,

stabilize performance, then validate the
whole thing together.

The audit raised seven findings, from the
connection pool to the widget.
All seven now pass locally.
The reported results:

twelve hundred and nine backend tests,
seventeen proxy tests run separately,

two hundred and sixty-two frontend unit
tests, and seventeen browser journeys.
That is fifteen hundred and five.

To check the tests themselves, fixes were
deliberately broken ten times,
and each break was caught.

The capacity gate passed ten of ten
declared runs,

once with only twenty-five milliseconds to
spare.

A backup and restore rehearsal passed, and
exposed a permissions bug, now fixed.

The self-audit score moved from eighty and
a half to eighty-five point seven five.

These are local results, not independent
certification,
and hosted CI has not run yet.

This is my undergraduate portfolio
project,

built with AI coding assistants including
Codex and Claude Code,

so I will not claim every line was typed
by hand.
What I want you to judge is the process:

written requirements with explicit
acceptance rules,

a baseline before changes, an audit,
focused fixes with retained failures,

and decisions held for approval instead of
assumed.
Ask me about any trade-off in this video,

including the ones that did not work out
the first time.
Where it stands:

the core engineering is validated locally
and all seven audit findings pass.

One migration policy decision still blocks
formal milestone closure.

Real AI evaluation, semantic answer
quality,

hosted CI and production deployment all
remain open.

Those are the roadmap, not existing
features,

which is why you are watching a controlled
demonstration rather than an always-on
public service.

A multi-tenant AI customer support
platform with retrieval augmented
generation.

Software engineering, full-stack
development and AI engineering.

The full case study, with its evidence and
its limitations,
is on my portfolio at venuja dot online.
Thank you for watching.
